accuracy.reason: All nine objectives preserve their scope: known-key access is neither a cache role nor a durability guarantee; explicit replacement semantics distinguish absence from unknown results; identity is not authorization; index maintenance, conditional writes, retry identity, removal rules, and distributed read modes are accurately bounded. Live AWS documentation and primary followups support these distinctions.

evidence.quote: Start with what the caller knows: the key, and which value it needs.

mechanisms.reason: The get/replace/delete trace exposes whole-value replacement. Namespaced identities and the diagram show distinct records. The two-writer diagram traces one accepted version change and one rejection, then reread/recompute. Retry, scan/index, expiry and hot-key explanations identify state and causal consequences rather than naming features.

evidence.quote: The condition and the write must share the same atomic boundary.

coherence.reason: The three supplied prerequisites suffice. Model and operations precede key/value design and discovery; atomic conflict detection precedes uncertain retry reasoning. Lifetime and distributed guarantees then supply the final workload decision. Every card prerequisite and objective is covered, including local definitions of partition, consistency and durability.

evidence.quote: Evaluate load distribution, read visibility and failure survival separately.

decisions.reason: Known-key fit is weighed against scan, index maintenance and application join costs. The learner can choose value boundaries, authorize access, recover rejected writes, avoid blind uncertain increments, and check expiry and read/failure guarantees. The final selection requires explained workload-specific checks and measurement rather than promising speed from a label.

evidence.quote: A simple access model is useful when it matches the work and its required guarantees.

clarity.reason: Definitions, concrete replacement examples and the two-writer diagram make all objectives usable. Dense caveats on retry identity, expiry and distributed guarantees, with repeated implementation checks, impose some reading effort; still correct and sufficient for the stated audience.

evidence.quote: Atomic execution and harmless repetition are different guarantees.

outcomes.reason: Q1 specifies unambiguous tenant/device/record-kind identity and the complete jointly read settings value, distinguishes authoritative use from cache and checked durability, traces replacement to only mode loud and confirmed post-delete absence, keeps timeout unknown, and requires caller authorization. All five criteria are supported by cards 1-3.

Q2 separates region discovery from known equipment IDs, explains scan work over inspected entries and index-directed reads, accounts for region changes/deletion and index consistency ownership, and verifies actual index availability. All four criteria follow from card 4.

Q3 correctly derives 21 rather than 22, traces one version-7 write advancing the version and the other rejected, preserves the second increment through reread/recompute and a conditional retry, and explains the separate-check race. Card 5 and its diagram support every criterion.

Q4 preserves unknown execution, compares identical replacement under the no-intervening-write premise with duplicate atomic increments, and requires verified same-operation identity with atomic effect/marker coordination or reconciliation without blind repetition. It distinguishes TTL and capacity eviction, denies retention/refresh/exact-time execution promises, and names product/configuration checks. Cards 6-7 support all six criteria.

Q5 defines keyspace partition locally, explains distributed many-key work and concentrated single-key capacity, separates stale permitted replica reads from acknowledged-data survival, and requires implementation/configuration/mode verification. All five criteria are explicitly supported by card 8.

Q6 fits A to a known independent record and explains scan/index/duplication/application-join costs for B. Authorization and durability are each selected and justified for A, and the answer rejects model-only performance or safety guarantees while recommending representative measurement. Cards 1,3,4,8,9 support all criteria.

sourceChecks.claim: Live CoreComponents verifies unique primary-key item identity and attribute values, while WorkingWithItems confirms scalar/set/document values and CRUD. ReadConsistency separately states DynamoDB persistence and read-mode guarantees; these are product promises, so the lesson correctly refuses to infer durability or disposable-cache use from the generic access model.

Live GetItem verifies lookup by complete key, no Item for a missing match, and selectable consistency. WorkingWithItems and ConditionExpressions verify whole-item put overwrite, deletion and operations distinct from failed/unknown replies. The deck explicitly specifies the replacement example and an observing read; it does not universalize all APIs.

Live fine-grained IAM conditions distinguish item keys from policies that allow or deny access to items and attributes. CoreComponents verifies unique primary-key identity; NoSQL design guidance relates data shape and size to access patterns. The tenant/account/kind tuple and explicit escaping are sound design deductions; the diagram never treats a namespace as permission.

Live SecondaryIndexes verifies alternate lookup keys, copied primary keys, automatic maintenance on insert/change/delete, and distinct consistency/capacity costs. The linked Scan followup confirms filtering occurs after reads and does not reduce consumed read capacity. The deck correctly requires checking product index support and maintenance responsibility.

Live ConditionExpressions verifies false predicates reject writes and matching predicates permit them. WorkingWithItems confirms atomic CRUD, tests against the latest item, and explicitly traces one concurrent update succeeding while the other fails. This supports the lesson version-and-value transition, rejection/reread/recompute path, and the insufficiency of a separate check.

Live Programming.Errors confirms uncertain single-item write execution, state/condition checks before retry, product-scoped request-token idempotency and backoff. WorkingWithItems explicitly says atomic counters are not idempotent and retries can double them. Previously live-inspected AWS Builders Library idempotent-API guidance supplies same caller intent, atomic token/effect coordination and retention requirements; no universal token feature is promised.

Live TTL documents delayed background deletion, expired items still pending deletion, and filtering expired results, supporting the warning about visibility and exact-time work. Previously live-inspected Redis eviction documentation ties capacity removal to maxmemory/policy and permits eviction of TTL-bearing entries. Expiry/eviction alone supply neither retention, replacement loading nor business execution.

Live partition-key design guidance recommends uniform activity, bounds serving partition capacity and gives a single-item throughput example. Partitions and data distribution explains key hashing into replicated storage partitions. ReadConsistency explicitly separates durably persisted successful writes from eventual reads that may omit recent writes, supporting separate configuration/read-mode and durability checks.

Live general NoSQL design guidance requires access-pattern-driven schemas, discusses costly unsupported queries, related-data grouping, traffic distribution and alternate indexes. Combined with live Scan/SecondaryIndexes facts it supports the stated costs of discovery and maintained alternate access. The lesson presents a workload decision and measurements, without copying the source page broader promotional performance claims.
